title: The Informational Cost of Structure: Representational Complexity in Networked Dynamical Systems
authors: Cyril Rommens, Pietro Traversa, Guilherme Ferraz de Arruda, Yamir Moreno
abstract: How much information is required to represent a dynamical system in terms of an interaction structure and an evolution rule? We address this question using algorithmic information theory. We introduce Representational Complexity, the excess description length of a structure-plus-rule model relative to the shortest possible description of the dynamics itself. This intrinsic description defines a universal lower bound: no exact structural representation can be more concise. If arbitrary rules are allowed, graphs, hypergraphs, and other formalisms can all reach this bound by shifting information between structure and dynamics, so expressiveness alone cannot distinguish them. Meaningful differences arise only when scientific modeling restricts the admissible structures and rules. Within this setting, we identify conditions under which graph and hypergraph descriptions are informationally equivalent, and show how graph-preferred, hypergraph-preferred, and mixed regimes can emerge when those conditions are relaxed. Because Kolmogorov complexity is not computable, we complement the formal results with explicit description-length estimates. Our framework reframes the choice of network representation as a question of informational cost and mechanistic transparency rather than universal expressive power.
summary: This theoretical work quantifies the informational overhead associated with choosing a model representation (like graph vs. hypergraph) for describing dynamical systems. By using algorithmic information theory, it shows that when interactions are inherently multi-body ($k \ge 3$), forcing them into a simple pairwise structure leads to an unrecoverable loss of information and thus a higher computational cost.
main_problem: The paper addresses the informational cost required to represent a complex dynamical system using an explicit interaction structure (like graphs or hypergraphs) coupled with an evolution rule.
main_result: Representational Complexity quantifies this cost, showing that for genuinely many-body interactions ($k \ge 3$), forcing the model into a pairwise graph representation incurs a measurable and non-zero informational penalty compared to using the native hypergraph structure.
method: The authors employ Algorithmic Information Theory (Kolmogorov Complexity) to define Representational Complexity, comparing description lengths between different structural models (e.g., Graph vs. Hypergraph).
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on finite Boolean dynamical maps $F: \{0, 1\}^N 	o \{0, 1\}^N$ operating on networked systems. The comparison is drawn between pairwise interactions (graphs) and higher-order interactions (hypergraphs).
key_observables: Representational Complexity ($	ext{RC}$), the difference in description length ($\Delta L$) between graph and hypergraph models.
important_parameters: The order of interaction ($k$), system size ($N$), and the number/type of interactions ($M$).
main_assumptions: Kolmogorov complexity is uncomputable, necessitating the use of computable description-length surrogates; equivalence results are conditional on specific structural recoverability assumptions.
figures_summary: The notes detail comparisons showing $\Delta L < 0$ (Graph preferred) for certain structures and $\Delta L > 0$ (Hypergraph preferred) when interactions require more than pairwise connections, such as in the clique expansion example.
paper_structure: The paper establishes Representational Complexity ($	ext{RC}$) as a fundamental measure. It first shows that expressiveness alone is insufficient to distinguish model types. Subsequently, it provides explicit comparisons (e.g., Graph vs. Hypergraph) demonstrating when structural assumptions lead to quantifiable informational overhead.
why_interesting: The concept of 'informational cost' for structure selection directly relates to identifying the minimal set of physical constraints needed to describe a complex system, which is crucial in modeling emergent behavior in many-body quantum systems or classical statistical mechanics models.
